calibrate-zpd.name: Calibrate to the zone of proximal development
calibrate-zpd.short: Set the task just past what they can do alone. If they finish it easily, raise it a step rather than repeating the level.

hold-standard.name: Hold the standard, don't dismiss the fear
hold-standard.short: Both at once. "That sounds real, and we're still doing it. What would make it possible?" Never "you'll be fine" (dismisses) or "okay, skip it" (lowers).

inclusive-excellence.name: Inclusive excellence
inclusive-excellence.short: More opportunity to get good, never a lower bar. Stassun's Fisk-Vanderbilt bridge; Treisman's Berkeley calculus groups, which were harder than the regular course.

transparency-statement.name: Transparency statement
transparency-statement.short: "My intention here is ___." Dobson's policing study: no explanation and 70% of civilians felt threatened; one opening sentence doubled conversation length.

wise-feedback.name: Wise feedback
wise-feedback.short: "I have high standards, and I'm giving you this feedback because I know you can meet them." Revision rates went 17% to 71%; among low-trust students, 0% to 82%.

correct-without-characterizing.name: Correct without characterizing
correct-without-characterizing.short: Never say anything negative about the person. Address the work, the situation or the feeling. The standard stays; the insult goes.

ask-dont-tell.name: Ask, don't tell
ask-dont-tell.short: Authentic (you don't know the answer), uptake (your follow-up uses their words), collaborative ("so we can fix it"). Matters most when correcting and when angry.

presume-agency.name: Presume agency, then hand over the thing
presume-agency.short: Respect autonomy, then presume agency, then give responsibility. They run it, not attend it.

long-term-commitment.name: Assure long-term commitment
long-term-commitment.short: If they fail: "We're going to keep working on this. I'm not going anywhere."

honor-status.name: Honor their status, never invoke yours
honor-status.short: If you're tempted to say "because I'm the adult", say what you actually need and why.

recruit-values.name: Recruit their values instead of forbidding
recruit-values.short: Prohibition raises the status of the thing prohibited. Align the behaviour with autonomy, status and fairness instead. Bryan et al. 2016, PNAS — 536 eighth graders.

validate-explain.name: Validate and explain, don't diminish
validate-explain.short: "That makes sense to be frustrated about. Here's what's behind it."

purpose-now.name: Purpose now, and make the argument broad
purpose-now.short: Future payoffs don't move adolescents; present meaning does. And narrow relevance excludes most of the room.

self-generated-writing.name: Self-generated writing
self-generated-writing.short: The student writes the argument. If the adult delivers it the mechanism is gone — they can discount you, they can't discount themselves.

people-can-change.name: People can change
people-can-change.short: Target the belief that character is fixed. Yeager's work here is on adolescent aggression and bullying.

stress-reappraisal.name: Stress reappraisal
stress-reappraisal.short: The racing heart is the body delivering oxygen — the system working, not failing. Raise the resources; don't lower the demand.

synergistic-mindsets.name: Synergistic mindsets
synergistic-mindsets.short: Growth mindset plus stress reappraisal, together. Teach that ability grows but not that the strain is useful, and the difficulty reads as proof they can't.

do-over.name: The do-over
do-over.short: If you broke the standard, go back, apologise for not upholding it, and ask curious, authentic questions. Implementation failure is guaranteed.

six-questions.name: The six questions
six-questions.short: Their meaning: what does this mean to you, how does that feel, does it serve your goals. Then an alternative meaning, and the same two questions again.

scenarios.scenario: Marcus, 11, finishes the twelve long-division problems you set in under four minutes and every one is right. He's spinning his pencil and looking around the room. There are eighteen minutes of the lesson left.
scenarios.modelAnswer: You got all twelve, and fast. So those aren't the ones for you any more. Here's one with a remainder that doesn't come out clean — I want to see how you handle it when the numbers stop being tidy.
rubric: Named that the current level is done rather than praising speed
Moved up a step instead of setting more of the same
Made the new task specific enough that he knows what is different about it

failureModes.enforcer: If you're finished, do the next twelve.
failureModes.protector: Nice work! You can read quietly until the others catch up.
failureModes.silent: Try this one instead.

scenarios.explanation: More of a task he has finished is not practice, it is waiting. Repeating a level he has cleared teaches him that speed is punished with volume.

scenarios.scenario: You coach under-14 football. Priya has nailed the drill you set — ten controlled touches against the wall, both feet, no drops. She looks up for what's next, slightly out of breath.
scenarios.modelAnswer: That's clean. Now do it with someone closing you down — I'll come at you, and you keep the same ten touches. It's going to fall apart the first few times, and that's the point of it.
rubric: Confirmed the current level is met
Added one variable rather than restarting or repeating
Told her in advance that failure at the new level is expected

failureModes.enforcer: Again. Twenty this time.
failureModes.protector: Perfect — take a water break, you've earned it.
failureModes.silent: Okay, now with pressure.

scenarios.explanation: Warning her the new level will break is what stops the first failure reading as a verdict. It reframes the difficulty as the design.

scenarios.scenario: Dominic, 23, is three months into his first analyst job. He's produced a flawless version of the same weekly report for six weeks. He's asked you twice whether there's anything else he could pick up.
scenarios.modelAnswer: You've made that report boring, which is the goal. So it's not your work any more — I want you to hand it to whoever comes in next and teach them to do it. Meanwhile you're taking the client summary, which you will not get right first time.
rubric: Treated mastery as the reason to move rather than the reason to keep him there
Raised the level rather than adding more volume at the same level
Was explicit that the new work will not go smoothly at first

failureModes.enforcer: Take the client summary as well as the report.
failureModes.protector: You're doing great — let's revisit in a few months once you're really settled.
failureModes.silent: Start on the client summary this week.

scenarios.explanation: Six weeks of flawless output is a signal the task is below him. Leaving someone at a level they have cleared reads as a judgement about what they are capable of.

scenarios.scenario: Aisha, 16, is down to present her project to the class in two days. She comes to you after the bell, arms folded, and says she genuinely cannot stand up in front of everyone and would rather take the zero.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I believe you that it feels impossible — that's not me doubting you. And you're still presenting. So tell me what would make it possible. Smaller room? Notes in your hand? Me standing at the back?
rubric: Took the fear seriously instead of arguing with it
Kept the requirement in place in the same breath
Turned it into a joint problem by asking what would make it possible

failureModes.enforcer: Everyone presents. That's the assignment.
failureModes.protector: Okay — you can hand in a written version instead.
failureModes.silent: You'll present on Thursday.

scenarios.explanation: "You'll be fine" dismisses the fear; "you can skip it" lowers the bar and tells her you agree she can't. Holding both is the whole mentor move in one sentence.

scenarios.scenario: Your 13-year-old, Theo, has a grading in his martial arts club on Saturday. On Thursday night he tells you at the kitchen table that he's not going, that he'll fail in front of everyone, and that he never wanted to grade anyway.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Failing in front of people you know is a genuinely bad feeling, and I'm not going to pretend it isn't. You're still going Saturday. What's the bit you're most worried about — is it the forms or the sparring? Let's work that bit tonight.
rubric: Named the fear as legitimate rather than talking him out of it
Restated the commitment without negotiating it away
Moved straight to what specifically would reduce the risk

failureModes.enforcer: You signed up. You're going.
failureModes.protector: There'll be another grading in six months — no shame in waiting.
failureModes.silent: We're leaving at nine on Saturday.

scenarios.explanation: "I never wanted to anyway" is usually the exit a young person builds when they expect to fail. Accepting it hands them the exit and confirms the expectation.

scenarios.scenario: Nadia, 24, is your direct report. She's been asked to run the client call on Friday because you'll be away. She emails at 11pm saying she doesn't think she's ready and asks you to move the call.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Not feeling ready for your first one is the correct feeling — I'd be worried if you felt nothing. The call is still Friday and it's still yours. Send me your three worst-case questions tonight and we'll build the answers before I go.
rubric: Validated the feeling as appropriate rather than as a problem
Left the responsibility with her instead of taking it back
Gave a concrete piece of preparation with a deadline attached

failureModes.enforcer: It's on the calendar. You'll manage.
failureModes.protector: No problem, I'll move it to next week when I'm back.
failureModes.silent: The call stays Friday. Prep the FAQs.

scenarios.explanation: Taking the call back is the protector move and it is expensive: it tells her that her own read on her readiness is the one you trust.

scenarios.scenario: Four students in your Year 10 maths set are consistently a grade behind the rest. Another teacher suggests you give them a shortened version of the end-of-term paper so they don't get demoralised.
scenarios.modelAnswer: They sit the same paper. What I'll do instead is run a Tuesday session where those four work the hardest problems together, out loud, with me there. Not easier questions — more chances at the real ones.
rubric: Refused to lower the assessment standard
Added opportunity rather than subtracting difficulty
Made the extra provision structured and specific rather than vague offers of help

failureModes.enforcer: They sit the same paper as everyone else. If they're behind, that's on them.
failureModes.protector: Good idea — a shorter paper will give them a win.
failureModes.silent: Same paper. I'll put on a Tuesday session.

scenarios.explanation: Treisman found Black students at Berkeley weren't failing calculus from ability or motivation, they were studying alone. His answer was group work harder than the course, not easier.

scenarios.scenario: You run a summer coding programme. A funder asks you to publish a lower entry threshold for applicants from under-resourced schools, to widen the intake and improve your diversity numbers.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I don't want a second threshold — the moment there are two bars, everyone knows who came in under which one, including the students. Fund me a four-week pre-programme instead and I'll get more of those applicants over the same bar.
rubric: Rejected the two-tier standard explicitly
Named the cost to the students themselves, not just the principle
Proposed added preparation as the alternative route to the same outcome

failureModes.enforcer: The bar is the bar. If they can't clear it they aren't ready.
failureModes.protector: We can lower it for those schools — it's only fair given what they're up against.
failureModes.silent: Let's do a pre-programme instead.

scenarios.explanation: Stassun's Fisk-Vanderbilt bridge became the largest US producer of Black and Latino physics and astronomy PhDs without lowering an admissions standard. The bridge did the work.

scenarios.scenario: Two 12-year-olds join your orchestra mid-year with much less playing experience than the rest. The conductor suggests giving them simplified parts so they can keep up in Friday's rehearsal.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Same parts. I'll take them for twenty minutes before rehearsal on Fridays and we'll work the two passages that will catch them out. They'll be behind for about a month and then they won't be.
rubric: Kept the same music rather than issuing an easier version
Created dedicated extra time rather than reducing the demand
Set an expectation that being behind is temporary and normal

failureModes.enforcer: They took the place, they play the part.
failureModes.protector: Simplified parts for now — no point setting them up to fail.
failureModes.silent: They'll play the full parts. I'll do Fridays with them.

scenarios.explanation: A simplified part is visible to everyone in the room including the two holding it. The message it sends outlasts the rehearsal.

scenarios.scenario: You need to sit down with Leo, 15, about the three lessons he's missed this fortnight. He walks in already braced, hands in his pockets, not sitting down.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Before anything else — my intention here isn't to catch you out or put anything on your record. I want to know what's going on those mornings so I can be useful about it. Sit down?
rubric: Stated the intention before raising the subject
Named what the conversation is not, given what he is clearly expecting
Kept it to one sentence rather than a speech

failureModes.enforcer: Three lessons missed. Explain.
failureModes.protector: Everything alright? No pressure, only if you want to talk.
failureModes.silent: Take a seat. Let's talk about the missed lessons.

scenarios.explanation: Dobson's study: officers who approached with no explanation left 70% of civilians feeling threatened. Officers who opened with one sentence of intent had conversations twice as long. Same officers.

scenarios.scenario: You're about to give your 19-year-old apprentice, Ben, a piece of hard feedback about how he spoke to a customer. He's seen you walking over and has gone quiet and still behind the counter.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I'm going to say something about the exchange with the woman at four o'clock. I'm telling you rather than writing it down because I want you to be able to argue with me about it. Alright?
rubric: Said what the conversation is for before starting it
Explained why it is being handled this way rather than another way
Invited a response instead of delivering a verdict

failureModes.enforcer: We need to talk about how you spoke to that customer.
failureModes.protector: Only a small thing — don't worry about it too much.
failureModes.silent: About the customer at four — you were short with her.

scenarios.explanation: P3: anything left unsaid between an authority and a non-authority gets guessed at, and the guess runs negative. Silence about your motive is not neutral.

scenarios.scenario: You're a new manager. On your second day you start dropping in on the team's client calls to learn the work. By day four you notice people going quiet when you join, and one person has started sending you notes before calls.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I should have said this on day one and didn't. I'm sitting in on calls because I don't know how you do this yet and I need to learn it — I'm not assessing anyone. If that's not landing, tell me and I'll stop.
rubric: Named the intention explicitly rather than assuming it was obvious
Acknowledged the silence had already been filled with a worse explanation
Left them a real way to push back

failureModes.enforcer: I'll be on calls this month. It's how I get up to speed.
failureModes.protector: Don't mind me — I'll stop joining if it's awkward.
failureModes.silent: I'll keep joining calls this week.

scenarios.explanation: The behaviour was already ambiguous for four days, and the team had filled the gap. A transparency statement works late, but it works better on day one.

scenarios.scenario: Sofia, 15, hands you a draft essay. It's underdeveloped — the argument doesn't hold and the evidence is thin. She's watching your face while you read it.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I'm giving you these comments because I have very high standards and I know you can reach them. The argument in paragraph three is where it comes apart — let's start there.
rubric: Stated the reason for the feedback before the feedback itself
Named a high standard and expressed belief she can meet it
Gave a specific, actionable next step rather than a general verdict

failureModes.enforcer: This isn't good enough. Rewrite it.
failureModes.protector: This is a really good start! Maybe just tighten paragraph three a bit.
failureModes.silent: Paragraph three doesn't hold up. Fix the argument and resubmit.

scenarios.explanation: Criticism is ambiguous. A student who suspects you think less of them reads red ink as a verdict on their ability. The sentence removes the ambiguity.

scenarios.scenario: You've watched Jamal, 17, shoot for twenty minutes. His release is late and it's costing him. He's the only one who stayed behind after training and he's clearly waiting to hear what you think.
scenarios.modelAnswer: The shot is fundamentally good — that's why I'm going to be picky about it. Your release is a beat late. I'm telling you because you're close enough to the right thing that the details are now worth fixing.
rubric: Affirmed the underlying standard is already high
Explained that the precision of the criticism is a consequence of that
Named the one specific thing to change

failureModes.enforcer: Your release is late. Fix it.
failureModes.protector: Looking good out there — keep at it.
failureModes.silent: Release a fraction earlier and that goes in.

scenarios.explanation: Engelland's version with draft picks: tell them the shot is fundamentally good, then refine the details ruthlessly. The affirmation is what buys the ruthlessness.

scenarios.scenario: Chloe, 22, has sent you a deck for a client. It's late, it's her third attempt, and it's still not right. She's added a note: "I think this one's there but tell me if not."
scenarios.modelAnswer: It's not there, and I'm going to keep sending it back, because the standard for what goes to a client is high and you're going to be the person who meets it. Slide 6 is the problem: it states the finding but never says what they should do about it.
rubric: Was direct that the work does not meet the bar
Framed continued feedback as belief rather than as disappointment
Located the exact failure rather than judging the whole deck

failureModes.enforcer: Still not right. Try again.
failureModes.protector: Nearly there — I'll just tidy the last bits myself.
failureModes.silent: Slide 6 needs a recommendation, not just the finding.

scenarios.explanation: By a third attempt, silence about your reasons has had three chances to be read as "she thinks I can't do this." Saying the standard out loud is what stops that.

scenarios.scenario: Ravi, 12, has just taken a wild shot from an impossible angle with two teammates unmarked in front of goal. He jogs back past you not making eye contact.
scenarios.modelAnswer: How did that feel?
rubric: Said nothing negative about him or the shot
Opened with a genuine question rather than a verdict
Left him to produce the assessment himself

failureModes.enforcer: That was a terrible shot. Pass the ball.
failureModes.protector: Unlucky! Good effort though.
failureModes.silent: Two players were open on your left.

scenarios.explanation: Engelland's question. A negative characterization delivers social pain, and once that lands nothing else in the conversation gets heard. The demand to fix the shot stays; the insult goes.

scenarios.scenario: Ellie, 13, shows you a maths answer that is confidently and completely wrong. Two other students are standing at your desk waiting.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Can you tell me how you got this?
rubric: Did not label the answer or the student as wrong
Asked about the method rather than the result
Made the next move hers rather than delivering the correction

failureModes.enforcer: That's wrong. Do it again.
failureModes.protector: Close! Have another look at the second line.
failureModes.silent: Check your second line.

scenarios.explanation: Estrada's question. "Wrong" is a verdict delivered in front of two onlookers; "how did you get this" is an invitation to find it, and usually she does.

scenarios.scenario: In a team meeting a 24-year-old on your team says something dismissive about a colleague who isn't in the room. Four other people heard it.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I'd rather we didn't do that about someone who isn't here to answer it. What's the actual problem with the handover? Let's solve that bit.
rubric: Addressed the behaviour without characterizing him in front of the others
Named the standard about absent colleagues rather than about his character
Redirected straight to the underlying problem

failureModes.enforcer: That's out of order. Don't talk about colleagues like that.
failureModes.protector: I think we're all a bit frustrated — let's move on.
failureModes.silent: Let's stick to the handover.

scenarios.explanation: The rule extends past correction: it governs how you speak about third parties in front of them. Publicly characterizing him would model exactly what you're objecting to.

scenarios.scenario: Stef, 14, has been stuck on the same coursework page for three days and has stopped asking for help. You sit down next to her.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Can you tell me where you're getting stuck and what you've tried, so we can fix the problem?
rubric: Asked rather than diagnosed
Asked about both the sticking point and what she has already attempted
Framed it as joint work — "so we can"

failureModes.enforcer: You've had three days. What have you actually done?
failureModes.protector: Don't worry about it — I'll walk you through the whole thing.
failureModes.silent: Where are you stuck?

scenarios.explanation: The "we" is the technique. Without it the same question is an audit. Three days of silence usually means she has stopped believing help is available without cost.

scenarios.scenario: You've asked your 16-year-old to be home by eleven. He comes in at ten past one, phone dead, no message. You are genuinely angry and he is standing in the hallway waiting for it.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I'm angry, so I'm going to ask instead of tell. What happened tonight?
rubric: Named the anger rather than acting it out
Converted the moment into a question
Asked an open question he could actually answer

failureModes.enforcer: Two hours late and not one message. You're not going out next weekend.
failureModes.protector: I'm just glad you're safe — get some sleep.
failureModes.silent: What happened?

scenarios.explanation: If you feel anger rising, ask a question instead of making a statement. Naming it out loud is what makes the question land as restraint rather than as a trap.

scenarios.scenario: A 21-year-old on your team missed a deadline that made you look bad in front of a client. In your one-to-one he opens with "I know, I messed up, I'll do better." You suspect there's more to it.
scenarios.modelAnswer: You said you'd do better — better how, specifically? I'm asking because I genuinely don't know what got in the way, and I'd rather fix that than have you promise harder.
rubric: Asked a question he could not answer with an apology
Made clear the question was authentic rather than rhetorical
Aimed at the obstacle rather than at his effort or character

failureModes.enforcer: Doing better isn't a plan. What's the plan?
failureModes.protector: These things happen — let's put it behind us.
failureModes.silent: What got in the way?

scenarios.explanation: A question you already know the answer to is a quiz. "I genuinely don't know" is what makes this authentic, and authenticity is what gets past the apology reflex.

scenarios.scenario: Your Year 8 form has a charity week coming up. In previous years you have planned it, assigned the roles, and run it. Two students have asked whether they can "help with" it this year.
scenarios.modelAnswer: You're not helping with it, you're running it. Pick your team, bring me the plan on Friday, and tell me what you need from me. I'll be there but it's yours.
rubric: Handed over the thing itself rather than a supporting role
Set a checkpoint rather than a set of instructions
Asked what they need from the adult, rather than telling them what the adult will do

failureModes.enforcer: You can do posters and collections. I'll handle the rest.
failureModes.protector: That's lovely — but it's a lot of work, so let me do the organising.
failureModes.silent: Sure, you two can run it.

scenarios.explanation: The strongest of the three levels: they run it, not attend it. Yeager's counterintuitive claim is that this saves the adult time, because responsibility actually transfers.

scenarios.scenario: Kofi, 17, has a mock exam in three weeks and a habit of revising by rereading his notes, which isn't working. You've told him twice what to do instead and nothing changed.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I've told you twice and that clearly isn't the thing that works, so I'll stop. What are you going to do differently for these three weeks? Tell me the plan and I'll tell you where I think it's thin.
rubric: Stopped assigning the method after it had failed twice
Asked what he is going to do rather than instructing him
Kept a role — reviewing the plan — without taking the plan over

failureModes.enforcer: Rereading doesn't work. Use past papers. Third time I've said it.
failureModes.protector: However you revise is fine, as long as you're doing something.
failureModes.silent: Try past papers instead.

scenarios.explanation: Presuming agency is the middle level: ask what they're going to do rather than assigning it. Telling him a third time would mostly demonstrate that telling is your only move.

scenarios.scenario: Your 10-year-old has to be at swimming at 7am on Saturdays. Every week you wake her, pack her bag, and chase her to the car, and every week it's a fight.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I'm going to stop running Saturday mornings. It's your session — set your own alarm, pack your bag Friday night. I'll drive at ten to seven whether or not you're ready, and I'm not going to nag you between now and then.
rubric: Transferred the actual responsibility, not just the chore
Stated the reason for the change rather than issuing it as a punishment
Named exactly what the adult will and will not do

failureModes.enforcer: If you're not in the car at ten to seven you're not going. Your choice.
failureModes.protector: I'll keep doing it — it's easier than the argument.
failureModes.silent: You're setting your own alarm from now on.

scenarios.explanation: The same words can be a threat or a handover. What separates them is whether the adult explains the reason and then actually stops managing it.

scenarios.scenario: Amara, 14, has failed the same music theory grade for the second time. She's sitting on the stairs outside the exam room with the result in her hand and won't look up.
scenarios.modelAnswer: We're going to keep working on this. I'm not going anywhere.
rubric: Signalled the relationship continues past the failure
Said nothing about the result itself or about her
Kept it short rather than filling the silence with analysis

failureModes.enforcer: Then we go again and this time you do the practice.
failureModes.protector: Honestly, grades aren't everything — maybe theory just isn't your thing.
failureModes.silent: Right. Let's look at what went wrong on Tuesday.

scenarios.explanation: The moment after a failure is when a young person decides whether the adult's interest was conditional on success. Everything else can wait until Tuesday.

scenarios.scenario: A 20-year-old you've been mentoring for a year gets rejected from the programme you helped her apply to. She messages: "Didn't get it. Sorry for wasting your time."
scenarios.modelAnswer: You didn't waste anything and I'm not going anywhere. Same time next month — we'll work out what the next one is when you've had a week to be annoyed about this one.
rubric: Rejected the framing that the relationship was contingent on the outcome
Committed to continuing, with something concrete attached
Allowed room for the disappointment rather than rushing to the next step

failureModes.enforcer: So what's the plan for the next application?
failureModes.protector: Their loss! You were far too good for it anyway.
failureModes.silent: No problem. Let me know when you want to look at other options.

scenarios.explanation: "Sorry for wasting your time" is the belief being tested. Answering the next-steps question instead leaves it untouched.

scenarios.scenario: Tyrone, 16, has been excluded for a week after an incident you weren't there for. On his first day back he comes to your room at break, stands in the doorway, and says "you probably don't want me in here."
scenarios.modelAnswer: You're in here. That hasn't changed and it isn't going to. Sit down — I don't need the story unless you want to tell it.
rubric: Answered the actual question, which was about whether he is still welcome
Made the commitment unconditional rather than tied to future behaviour
Did not require an account of the incident as the price of entry

failureModes.enforcer: You can be in here if you're straight with me about what happened.
failureModes.protector: Of course you can! It's all forgotten, don't think about it again.
failureModes.silent: Come in.

scenarios.explanation: He's testing whether the exclusion cost him the relationship. Attaching a condition — even a reasonable one — answers yes.

scenarios.scenario: Your 15-year-old refuses to turn his music down for the third time. You can feel "because I said so" arriving in your mouth.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I've got a call in ten minutes and I can hear the bass through the wall. I need it down until half past — after that I don't care how loud it is.
rubric: Said the actual reason instead of invoking authority
Made the request specific and bounded in time
Left him his standing rather than winning the exchange

failureModes.enforcer: Turn it down. Because I'm your father, that's why.
failureModes.protector: Never mind, I'll take the call in the car.
failureModes.silent: Turn it down please.

scenarios.explanation: "Because I'm the adult" spends your status to take his. From 10 to 25 the brain is intensely averse to humiliation, and the cost usually shows up later, in something unrelated.

scenarios.scenario: A 17-year-old challenges your marking in front of the class — not rudely, but publicly, and he has half a point.
scenarios.modelAnswer: You might be right about question four. Bring it to me at the end and if it holds up I'll change it — and I'll tell the class I changed it.
rubric: Conceded the possibility publicly rather than defending status
Set a real process rather than shutting it down
Offered to make the correction visible, which returns status rather than taking it

failureModes.enforcer: My marking isn't up for debate in the middle of a lesson.
failureModes.protector: You know what, fine — I'll give you the mark.
failureModes.silent: See me at the end.

scenarios.explanation: He has raised a claim in front of an audience. Defending your position costs you the class; conceding the process costs you nothing and buys the room.

scenarios.scenario: In a planning meeting, a 23-year-old on your team pushes back hard on your proposal in front of two senior colleagues. Her objection is wrong, but it isn't stupid.
scenarios.modelAnswer: That's the right question and I should have covered it. The reason it still works is the second contract — but say more about the timing risk, because I think you're onto something separate there.
rubric: Credited the question before correcting the conclusion
Gave the actual reason rather than asserting seniority
Found the part she was right about and handed it back to her

failureModes.enforcer: That's not how the contract works. Moving on.
failureModes.protector: Good point — let's park the whole thing and revisit.
failureModes.silent: The second contract covers it.

scenarios.explanation: She spent status to raise it in that room. Correcting her without returning any of it teaches everyone watching what pushing back costs.

scenarios.scenario: You run a Year 9 tutor group. Vaping in the toilets has become the thing. The assembly on the health risks last term visibly made it more popular.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Look at who makes money when you vape. They designed the flavours for you specifically, they bought the influencers you follow, and they are counting on you not noticing. You get to decide whether they get to run you.
rubric: Avoided prohibition or health warnings entirely
Framed the industry as the controlling party
Put the young person in the higher-status position of seeing through it

failureModes.enforcer: Anyone caught vaping is on report. No exceptions.
failureModes.protector: I know it's hard to resist when everyone's doing it.
failureModes.silent: There are health risks I want you to be aware of.

scenarios.explanation: Bryan, Yeager, Hinojosa et al. 2016, PNAS — 536 eighth graders read an exposé of food-industry marketing with executives framed as controlling and hypocritical. A day later, in an unrelated setting, they chose healthier snacks.

scenarios.scenario: Phones are out constantly in your sixth-form class. You've banned them, confiscated them, and made a rule about the box by the door. Nothing has worked for longer than a week.
scenarios.modelAnswer: These are built by people whose job is to take your attention and sell it. You're the product. I'd like this hour to be one where you decide what you're paying attention to instead of an app deciding for you.
rubric: Dropped the prohibition frame
Named the designer's intent rather than the student's weakness
Made attention a matter of autonomy rather than compliance

failureModes.enforcer: Phones in the box or I take them for the day.
failureModes.protector: I'd rather you didn't, but I know it's difficult.
failureModes.silent: Phones away for this hour, please.

scenarios.explanation: Prohibition raises the status of the thing prohibited. Direct anti-drug and anti-smoking messaging increased use — the ban is part of the appeal.

scenarios.scenario: Two 22-year-olds on your team keep skipping the security training because it's dull. You've reminded them twice and it's now a compliance issue you'll have to escalate.
scenarios.modelAnswer: The reason this exists is that the last breach in our sector leaked a client list of people who'd asked for confidentiality. You two are the ones who talk to those clients. I'd rather you did it because of that than because HR made you.
rubric: Connected the task to something they already care about
Avoided leading with the compliance threat
Gave them the choice explicitly rather than removing it

failureModes.enforcer: It's mandatory. Do it this week or it goes to HR.
failureModes.protector: I know it's tedious — I'll see if I can get you an extension.
failureModes.silent: Please complete the training this week.

scenarios.explanation: The same request lands differently depending on whether it appeals to fairness and autonomy or to the threat of an authority. Escalation is still available; it just stops being the first move.

scenarios.scenario: Mia, 11, is furious that she's been moved to a different table in class, away from her friend. To you it is a seating plan. To her it is the end of the world.
scenarios.modelAnswer: That makes complete sense to be upset about — you've sat with her since September. Here's what's behind it: I've split the four people who talk the most, and you're two of them. Let's look at it again at half term.
rubric: Validated the feeling as proportionate rather than as an overreaction
Gave the actual reason behind the decision
Offered a real future review point rather than a dismissal

failureModes.enforcer: It's a seating plan. You'll survive.
failureModes.protector: Oh — okay, you can move back if it's making you this unhappy.
failureModes.silent: You're on that table now. That's the plan.

scenarios.explanation: Adults routinely misjudge the size of a status event in a young person's life. The feeling is proportionate to the social stake, which is not the same as the adult's stake.

scenarios.scenario: Your 13-year-old is distraught about not being invited to something. You have a strong instinct to say it doesn't matter and they'll have forgotten by next week.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Being left out of something everyone's talking about is genuinely horrible, and I'm not going to tell you it isn't. It's also not information about whether people like you — it's information about one person's guest list.
rubric: Refused to minimise the feeling
Named the pain accurately rather than generically
Separated the event from the conclusion being drawn from it

failureModes.enforcer: You can't be invited to everything. That's life.
failureModes.protector: I'll message their mum and see what happened.
failureModes.silent: Their loss. Want to do something Saturday?

scenarios.explanation: "It doesn't matter" is heard as "you are wrong to feel this," which ends the conversation. Explaining what the event does and does not mean leaves it open.

scenarios.scenario: A 24-year-old on your team is visibly annoyed that a project she led is being presented by someone else at the board meeting. She says "it's fine, honestly."
scenarios.modelAnswer: It's not fine and it makes sense to be annoyed — you did the work. The reason is that the board asked for the finance lead specifically, and that's a rule about the meeting, not about you. Your name is on the paper and I'll say it in the room.
rubric: Named the feeling she was suppressing rather than accepting "it's fine"
Explained the actual mechanism behind the decision
Did something concrete about the underlying issue of credit

failureModes.enforcer: That's how board meetings work. It's not personal.
failureModes.protector: You're right, it's unfair — I'll push back and get you in the room.
failureModes.silent: The board asked for the finance lead. Your name's on the paper.

scenarios.explanation: "It's fine" is rarely fine, and taking it at face value is the silent move. The explanation is what stops her filling the gap with a story about her standing.

scenarios.scenario: A 14-year-old asks, not rudely, why he has to do algebra when he wants to be a mechanic.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Not because you'll use quadratics under a car. Doing hard abstract things makes your brain better at hard concrete things, and the people who can do both are the ones who end up running the garage instead of working in it.
rubric: Refused the narrow career-relevance argument
Gave a reason that applies now rather than in a distant future
Made the argument broad enough to include him rather than a specific job

failureModes.enforcer: Because it's on the syllabus and you need the grade.
failureModes.protector: Fair enough — focus on what you're good at.
failureModes.silent: It comes up more than you'd think in the trades.

scenarios.explanation: Future payoffs don't move adolescents; present meaning does. And "you'll use this in a finance job" excludes most of the room by design.

scenarios.scenario: You're introducing a history unit on the 1930s to a class of 15-year-olds. Last year the same lesson opened with "this will come up in your exam" and the room died.
scenarios.modelAnswer: This week you're not studying the 1930s, you're interviewing them. Everyone picks one person who was alive and works out what they knew and when they knew it. By Friday you'll be able to tell me what it feels like to not know how something ends.
rubric: Framed the work as something they do now rather than something that pays off later
Made the meaning available to any student rather than the exam-focused ones
Gave a concrete outcome for the week

failureModes.enforcer: This unit is worth 20% of the paper. Take it seriously.
failureModes.protector: I know this period is dry — we'll get through it quickly.
failureModes.silent: We're starting the 1930s. Open at page forty.

scenarios.explanation: "You're interviewing someone interesting" is the move. The exam still exists; it just stops being the reason offered.

scenarios.scenario: A 20-year-old on your team says the compliance paperwork she does all Thursday is pointless. You privately half agree with her.
scenarios.modelAnswer: About a third of it is genuinely box-ticking and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. The other two thirds is the only record that exists if a client disputes something, which has happened twice and both times that file is what protected the person who did the work. Let's cut the third that's noise.
rubric: Conceded the part of her objection that was correct
Gave a present, concrete reason for the part that matters
Acted on the complaint rather than only reframing it

failureModes.enforcer: It's not optional. Everyone does it.
failureModes.protector: You're right, it is pointless — just get through it.
failureModes.silent: It protects you if a client disputes something.

scenarios.explanation: A purpose argument that requires ignoring an accurate objection doesn't survive contact. Conceding the true third is what makes the other two thirds credible.

scenarios.scenario: Six weeks into Year 7, several students clearly think everyone else has settled in and they haven't. You could give an assembly about how normal that is.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Read these four accounts from last year's Year 7s about their first term. Then write a page to a Year 6 who's worried about September, telling them what you'd want them to know.
rubric: Had the students produce the argument rather than delivering it
Gave them real prior accounts as the input
Directed the writing at a younger audience rather than at the teacher

failureModes.enforcer: Everyone finds the first term hard. Get on with it.
failureModes.protector: If anyone's struggling to settle, my door is always open.
failureModes.silent: Here are some accounts from last year's Year 7s. Have a read.

scenarios.explanation: A student who doubts they belong can discount an adult — you have to say that. They cannot discount themselves. Walton & Cohen 2011, Science: the Black-white GPA gap cut 52% over three years, from one hour.

scenarios.scenario: You're writing the four stories students will read before they write their own. You have a draft that ends with the student's problems resolved and everything going well.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Rewrite the ending. It should show how the first steps compounded into more steps — not that the struggle stopped. A happy ending that promises the difficulty ends is one the reader will catch you on by November.
rubric: Kept the four-part structure: normalize, change is possible, action steps, snowball
Rejected an ending that promises the struggle ends
Explained why the overclaim would backfire

failureModes.enforcer: The stories need to be more realistic. Redo them.
failureModes.protector: It's nice and hopeful — leave it, they need encouragement.
failureModes.silent: Change the ending to show the steps compounding.

scenarios.explanation: The structure is normalize, change is possible, action steps, snowball. The snowball is compounding, not resolution — a story that promises the struggle ends gets disconfirmed and takes the rest with it.

scenarios.scenario: You want your sixth-formers to see why the course matters. Your instinct is a fifteen-minute talk on where the subject shows up in the world.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Two paragraphs each, this Friday: how something we've covered this term connects to something you actually care about. I'm not marking them and I'm not collecting them unless you want me to.
rubric: Had them generate the relevance rather than presenting it
Kept it short and low-stakes
Removed the assessment so the writing isn't performed for the teacher

failureModes.enforcer: Two paragraphs on why this matters, marked, due Friday.
failureModes.protector: I'll put together a slide on why this subject is useful.
failureModes.silent: Write two paragraphs on how this connects to something you care about.

scenarios.explanation: Hulleman and Harackiewicz ran this as one to two paragraphs, a few times a semester. The gains landed on students with low expectations of success and not on the rest.

scenarios.scenario: Yusuf, 13, has decided a boy in his year "is just a d---head" after an incident in the corridor, and has started avoiding a whole set of lessons to steer clear of him.
scenarios.modelAnswer: What he did was worth being angry about. Here's the thing I'd want you to hold though — people that age are still being built. Who he is in Year 9 isn't who he'll be, and that's true of you as well.
rubric: Did not defend or excuse the behaviour
Targeted the belief that the other person's character is fixed
Applied the same claim to the student himself rather than only to the other boy

failureModes.enforcer: You don't get to skip lessons because of him. Sort it out.
failureModes.protector: Some people are just difficult — stay out of his way.
failureModes.silent: He might grow out of it. Try not to let it stop you going to lessons.

scenarios.explanation: Yeager's work here is on aggression and bullying: the belief that people's character is fixed is what turns one incident into a permanent enemy and a changed timetable.

scenarios.scenario: A 16-year-old tells you she's given up on her relationship with her father because "he's always been like this and he's never going to change."
scenarios.modelAnswer: You might be right that he doesn't change. What I'd push back on is "never" — people do move, usually slowly and usually not because they were asked to. That doesn't obligate you to wait around for it. It just means the door doesn't have to be nailed shut.
rubric: Did not promise the other person will change
Challenged the fixed-character belief without dismissing her experience
Left her free to protect herself rather than prescribing reconciliation

failureModes.enforcer: He's your dad. You need to make an effort.
failureModes.protector: Then you're better off without him, honestly.
failureModes.silent: People do change sometimes.

scenarios.explanation: The belief being targeted is that character is fixed, not the question of whether she should forgive him. Over-promising change would be a claim you can't support.

scenarios.scenario: A 12-year-old says, about himself, "I'm just a bad kid, everyone knows it." He says it flatly, like a fact he's reporting.
scenarios.modelAnswer: You've done some things this term that got you in trouble. That's a list of things you did, which is different from a description of what you are. The first one changes. Which of them do you want off the list first?
rubric: Separated the behaviour from the identity
Did not deny the incidents happened
Turned it into a next action rather than a reassurance

failureModes.enforcer: Then stop doing bad things and people will stop saying it.
failureModes.protector: You're not a bad kid at all! Don't ever say that.
failureModes.silent: You're not a bad kid.

scenarios.explanation: "You're not a bad kid" contradicts what he believes everyone knows, so it reads as kindness rather than information. Separating the list from the label is checkable.

scenarios.scenario: Imani, 17, is outside the exam hall with her hands shaking. She says "I can't do this, look at me, I'm falling apart."
scenarios.modelAnswer: That's your body sending oxygen to your brain and your muscles. It's the delivery system switching on, not a sign anything's wrong. People perform better with it than without it — you're set up right.
rubric: Reframed the physical symptom as functional rather than as a warning
Did not tell her to calm down or ignore it
Connected the arousal to performing better, not merely to coping

failureModes.enforcer: Everyone's nervous. Go in and get on with it.
failureModes.protector: Take a minute — I can ask if you can sit this one later.
failureModes.silent: Try to breathe and ignore it. You'll be fine once you start.

scenarios.explanation: Jamieson et al. 2016: 93 community college developmental maths students across five semesters. The control group was told to ignore their stress — an active comparison, not nothing.

scenarios.scenario: A 19-year-old is about to give her first presentation to a room of forty. She's just told you her heart is pounding and she thinks she's going to be sick.
scenarios.modelAnswer: The pounding is exactly what a body does before it does something that matters — it's giving you more blood to the brain than you had ten minutes ago. You're better resourced right now than when you were calm.
rubric: Named the symptom as evidence of resources arriving
Avoided any instruction to relax or suppress
Framed her as better equipped, not merely as coping

failureModes.enforcer: Nerves are normal. You're on in five.
failureModes.protector: If it's too much, I can present and you can take questions.
failureModes.silent: Deep breaths. You'll be fine.

scenarios.explanation: Stress happens when demands exceed resources. The mentor raises the resources — reframing the arousal is raising them — rather than lowering the demand.

scenarios.scenario: A 25-year-old on your team is a week from a promotion panel. He says he's fine, but he's stopped sleeping and has asked you twice whether he can withdraw and go for it next cycle.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Not sleeping the week before something you want is your system taking it seriously. That response is what you'll be running on in the room, and it's an asset there. Withdrawing is available — I'd rather you decided that rested than at 3am.
rubric: Reappraised the symptom rather than treating it as evidence he isn't ready
Kept the demand in place rather than removing it
Did not dismiss the option, but named when the decision should be made

failureModes.enforcer: You're ready. Withdrawing would look worse than a bad panel.
failureModes.protector: Go next cycle — there's no rush and you'll be more confident.
failureModes.silent: Everyone feels like that before a panel.

scenarios.explanation: The threat response and the challenge response are the same arousal read two different ways. Which one he goes in with is partly decided by how it gets named beforehand.

scenarios.scenario: You've spent a term teaching your Year 10s that ability grows with effort. Several of the ones who most needed it are now visibly more discouraged after hard tasks, not less.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I've told you your brain grows when you struggle. I left out the other half: the horrible feeling when it's hard is the growing. If it felt comfortable it wouldn't be doing anything. Both things or neither.
rubric: Recognised that the growth message alone had backfired
Added the reappraisal of the strain specifically
Made explicit that the two only work delivered together

failureModes.enforcer: Effort is what matters. Keep going.
failureModes.protector: Let's do some easier tasks to rebuild confidence.
failureModes.silent: Struggle is part of learning.

scenarios.explanation: Teach that ability can grow but not that the strain of growing it is useful, and the difficulty reads as proof they can't. Yeager et al. 2022, Nature 607: a synergistic mindsets intervention protects adolescents from stress.

scenarios.scenario: A 21-year-old has been told all his life that he's a natural at this and is now failing at something for the first time. He's concluded he was never actually good.
scenarios.modelAnswer: You were never a natural, you were early. What you're feeling now is what the work costs, and everyone who got further than you paid it sooner. The strain is the price and it's also the mechanism — there isn't a version where you get better without it.
rubric: Attacked the fixed-ability story directly
Reframed the distress as the cost of growth rather than as evidence of a ceiling
Delivered both halves in the same breath

failureModes.enforcer: Talent only gets you so far. Now you have to work.
failureModes.protector: You're still one of the best here — this one was just a hard brief.
failureModes.silent: Everyone hits this point eventually.

scenarios.explanation: "Talent only gets you so far" is the growth half without the stress half, which is why it usually lands as an accusation rather than as help.

scenarios.scenario: Your 15-year-old daughter has started saying she's "just not a maths person" and has begun feeling sick before tests. Two separate things, or one.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Two things and they're feeding each other. Maths people aren't born, they're built, and the sick feeling before a test is your body getting ready rather than warning you. Believe the first without the second and every test feels like proof.
rubric: Identified the fixed-ability belief and the stress response as linked
Reframed both, not just one
Explained the mechanism by which they compound

failureModes.enforcer: There's no such thing as a maths person. Do the practice.
failureModes.protector: Not everyone's a maths person — play to your strengths.
failureModes.silent: You can definitely get better at maths.

scenarios.explanation: This is the exact pairing the Nature study tests. Addressing the belief while leaving the physiology unexplained leaves her with a theory that says she should be improving and a body that says she's failing.

scenarios.scenario: You lost your temper at your 14-year-old last night over an unwashed pan and said something sarcastic about how she treats the house like a hotel. She's been in her room since.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I want to go back to last night. The pan mattered a bit; what I said about you was out of order and it wasn't about the pan. I'm sorry. Can I ask what that landed like?
rubric: Went back to it explicitly rather than moving on
Apologised for the characterization, not for having a standard
Ended with a curious, authentic question

failureModes.enforcer: I shouldn't have shouted, but you did leave it there all day.
failureModes.protector: I'm sorry — forget the pan, it doesn't matter.
failureModes.silent: Sorry about last night.

scenarios.explanation: Seidel's do-over. Note what is not apologised for: the standard about the kitchen stands. What's withdrawn is the characterization of her.

scenarios.scenario: You told a 16-year-old in front of his class that if he didn't want to be there he could leave. He left. It's the next morning and he's back in your room.
scenarios.modelAnswer: I said something yesterday I shouldn't have, in front of everyone, and I'd have been furious if someone said it to me. I'm sorry. The work still needs doing — but what was actually going on yesterday?
rubric: Named the specific failure including that it was public
Apologised without conditioning it on his behaviour
Kept the standard and moved to an authentic question

failureModes.enforcer: You shouldn't have walked out. But I shouldn't have said it like that.
failureModes.protector: Let's forget yesterday ever happened.
failureModes.silent: Sorry about yesterday. Get your book out.

scenarios.explanation: Yeager calls this the most realistic tool in the book, because implementation failure is guaranteed. Even Estrada failed badly before adopting the mentor mindset.

scenarios.scenario: You dismissed a 23-year-old's idea in a meeting three weeks ago with a one-liner that got a laugh. She hasn't volunteered anything in a meeting since and you've only just connected the two.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Three weeks ago I got a laugh at the expense of your idea, and you haven't put anything forward since. That's on me and I'm sorry. What would need to be true for you to risk it again?
rubric: Named the specific incident and the consequence, without making her raise it
Took responsibility rather than framing it as a misunderstanding
Asked what would need to change rather than instructing her to contribute

failureModes.enforcer: You've gone quiet in meetings. I need you contributing.
failureModes.protector: You should speak up more — everyone values your input, honestly.
failureModes.silent: Sorry if that came across badly a few weeks back.

scenarios.explanation: "Sorry if it came across badly" puts the fault in her reception. The do-over requires naming what you actually did.

scenarios.scenario: Your 15-year-old is refusing to go to his grandmother's on Sunday. It's become a standoff and you've both said things about it twice this week.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Before we argue about Sunday again — what does going to Grandma's mean to you? … And how does that meaning make you feel? … Is feeling that serving what you actually want here?
rubric: Asked what it means to him before offering any alternative
Followed with how that meaning feels
Asked whether it serves his goals rather than yours

failureModes.enforcer: She's eighty-two and you're going. End of discussion.
failureModes.protector: Fine, stay home — I'll say you're revising.
failureModes.silent: Why don't you want to go?

scenarios.explanation: Round one is entirely about their meaning. Offering the alternative before the first three questions are answered turns the whole thing back into an argument with extra steps.

scenarios.scenario: You've asked the first three questions. Ade, 17, has told you that being made to attend the family event means he's still treated like a child, that it makes him resentful, and that no, it isn't serving him.
scenarios.modelAnswer: So here's another thing it could mean: that you're one of the few people who can actually talk to her. What would it feel like if that's what it was? And would that serve what you want?
rubric: Offered an alternative meaning rather than a rebuttal
Asked how the new meaning would feel before asking whether it works
Left him to accept or reject it rather than asserting it is the truth

failureModes.enforcer: It doesn't mean you're a child, it means you're family.
failureModes.protector: I hear you — you don't have to come.
failureModes.silent: Maybe think of it as her getting to see you rather than you being made to go.

scenarios.explanation: Round two mirrors round one exactly: another meaning, how that would feel, whether it serves the goal. The symmetry is what makes it a negotiation rather than a persuasion.

scenarios.scenario: You and your 18-year-old have reached the point where the argument about the car has stopped. Nobody has conceded; you're both just not raising it. She's about to leave the room.
scenarios.modelAnswer: We've stopped fighting about it but we haven't agreed anything. I want to know what you need for this to work, and I'll tell you what I need, and then we write down what we've actually agreed — including when we look at it again.
rubric: Named that stopping the fight is not the same as settling it
Put both sides' needs on the table rather than only stating terms
Built in renegotiation rather than treating the agreement as final

failureModes.enforcer: The rule stands. I don't want to hear about the car again.
failureModes.protector: Let's just drop it — it's not worth the arguing.
failureModes.silent: Let's agree some rules about the car.

scenarios.explanation: A truce ends fighting. A treaty establishes terms: both sides assess needs, both know what the other needs to thrive, terms are mutually agreed, and it gets renegotiated with the lines kept open.
